claims.text: The proposed alloy is a lightweight Mg-based alloy containing Ti, Zr, and Sc.
A two-stage sintering protocol can produce a dense, single-phase-like microstructure with superior barrier properties.
An 800–850 °C first stage forms a metastable solid solution while suppressing volatile-element loss.
A rapid 950–980 °C spike completes densification without extensive phase segregation or volatility.
The starting material is a mechanically alloyed mixture of 99.9% Mg and Ti, Zr, and Sc powders with average particle size below 20 µm.
Mechanical alloying ensures powder homogeneity.
Stage 1 is performed at 825 °C for 30 minutes with a 5 °C/min heating rate.
Stage 2 is performed at 975 °C for 5 minutes with a 20 °C/min heating rate.
Sintering is conducted by spark plasma sintering under 50 MPa in 99.999% argon containing less than 1 ppm oxygen.
The metastable solid solution formed during Stage 1 acts as a precursor to the single-phase-like microstructure formed during Stage 2.
The Stage 1 metastable solid solution suppresses elemental segregation and volatile loss.
The low-temperature stage limits diffusion to short-range ordering, thereby enabling metastable solid-solution formation.
The short high-temperature stage supplies sufficient energy for densification while leaving too little time for Mg escape or phase segregation.
The protocol will produce greater than 98% relative density.
The protocol will produce a single-phase-like microstructure with grain size below 5 µm.
The protocol will improve oxidation resistance by 50% and corrosion resistance in 3.5% NaCl by 40% relative to standard sintering.
Standard sintering at 900 °C for 60 minutes yields 92% relative density and a multiphase, segregated microstructure with poor oxidation and corrosion resistance.
Below 800 °C, densification fails because diffusion is insufficient.
Above 1000 °C, volatility causes Mg loss and porosity.
The useful sintering window is 800–1000 °C, with the proposed optimum represented by stages at 825 °C and 975 °C.
